original_value: Human–Robot interaction represents a cornerstone of mobile robotics, especially within the field of social robots. In this context, user localization becomes of crucial importance for the interaction. This work investigates the capabilities of wide field-of-view RGB cameras to estimate the 3D position and orientation (i.e., the pose) of a user in the environment. For that, we employ a social robot endowed with a fish-eye camera hosted in a tilting head and develop two complementary approaches: (1) a fast method relying on a single image that estimates the user pose from the detection of their feet and does not require either the robot or the user to remain static during the reconstruction; and (2) a method that takes some views of the scene while the camera is being tilted and does not need the feet to be visible. Due to the particular setup of the tilting camera, special equations for 3D reconstruction have been developed. In both approaches, a CNN-based skeleton detector (OpenPose) is employed to identify humans within the image. A set of experiments with real data validate our two proposed methods, yielding similar results than commercial RGB-D cameras while surpassing them in terms of coverage of the scene (wider FoV and longer range) and robustness to light conditions.

result.paraphrase: Human–Robot interaction is a key pillar of mobile robotics, particularly in social robotics, where locating the user is critical for effective interaction. This study explores how wide field-of-view RGB cameras can estimate a user’s 3D position and orientation, i.e., their pose, in the environment. To do so, we use a social robot equipped with a fish-eye camera mounted on a tilting head and devise two complementary methods: (1) a rapid single-image approach that infers user pose from foot detection and requires neither the robot nor the user to stay still during reconstruction; and (2) an approach that uses several views captured while the camera is tilting and does not require the feet to be visible. Because of the specific tilting-camera configuration, dedicated equations for 3D reconstruction were developed. In both methods, a CNN-based skeleton detector, OpenPose, is used to locate people in the image. Experiments with real data validate the proposed methods, showing performance similar to commercial RGB-D cameras while exceeding them in scene coverage, with a wider FoV and longer range, and in robustness to lighting conditions.
